material_facts.description: Davis had a prior 2022 left shoulder AC joint sprain and mild rotator cuff tendinitis from a motorcycle fall, treated with x-rays and a 12-session physical therapy course.
On 2024-01-08, Davis's left arm was crushed by an industrial metal stamping press at NSK plant, requiring EMS extrication, tourniquet application, and emergent transport to trauma care.
Davis was diagnosed with a complete traumatic amputation of the left arm between the shoulder and elbow with complete vascular and neurologic disruption and traumatic shock from blood loss.

Imaging showed comminuted open segmental fractures of the forearm/hand, a comminuted displaced supracondylar humerus fracture, and complete cessation of brachial artery contrast enhancement, confirming an unsalvageable limb.
Davis received an emergency transfusion of 2 units PRBC for traumatic blood loss/shock prior to surgery.
Dr. Marcus Vance performed an emergent left transhumeral (above-elbow) amputation with myofascial closure, bone beveling, and traction-neurectomy of the median, ulnar, and radial nerves.
Postoperative labs showed leukocytosis and anemia, with a urine drug screen positive only for trace cannabinoids and negative for ethanol.

Postoperative inpatient care included a multimodal pain regimen (Dilaudid PCA, gabapentin, prophylactic IV antibiotics, PRN oxycodone), JP drain placement and removal on POD4, with improving vitals and pain over the 7-day admission before discharge on oral pain medications.

At one-month follow-up, Davis developed severe phantom limb pain (8/10) and stump hypersensitivity, requiring increased gabapentin dosing and referral for desensitization therapy and prosthetic fitting.
At five months post-amputation, Davis developed a symptomatic post-amputation traumatic neuroma of the ulnar/median nerve stump causing electrical shock pain and interfering with prosthetic fitting.
Dr. Marcus Vance performed a stump revision surgery excising a 1.8 x 1.4 cm neuroma of the median/ulnar nerves with proximal nerve transposition and embedding into the triceps muscle.
Liberty Mutual placed prosthetic therapy authorization on hold pending peer review of the proposed myoelectric transhumeral prosthesis, suspending PT/OT sessions.

At rehab intake and PT evaluation following amputation and neuroma surgery, Davis had reduced left shoulder range of motion (abduction 120/180, flexion 130/180), ongoing phantom pain, poor sleep, and was off work.

Davis was fitted with a custom myoelectric left transhumeral prosthesis (carbon-fiber socket, Utah Myoelectric Elbow, Motion Control MC Hand), demonstrating 80% electrode signal control accuracy at initial fitting.

Davis underwent an extended physical therapy course (February 2025 to June 2026) at Hope Valley for prosthetic training, progressing through electrode control, grasping/ADL tasks, shoulder strengthening, and functional/vocational simulation with pain decreasing from 5/10 to 1/10.
Davis had two no-show PT appointments (attributed to workload and transportation issues) during the prosthetic training course.

Davis was discharged from physical therapy having achieved master-level operation of his myoelectric prosthesis, independent ADLs, driving, and carrying up to 25 lbs, with near-normal left shoulder ROM, and was released to modified light/medium duty work.
